explorer.polo.name: Marco Polo
explorer.polo.title: The Journey to Kublai Khan
explorer.polo.summary: A Venetian merchant's son travels with his father and uncle along the Silk Road to the court of Kublai Khan.
explorer.magellan.name: Ferdinand Magellan
explorer.magellan.title: The First Circumnavigation
explorer.magellan.summary: Five Spanish ships search for a western route to the Spice Islands. One returns, the first to sail around the world.
explorer.livingstone.name: David Livingstone
explorer.livingstone.title: Across Africa
explorer.livingstone.summary: A Scottish missionary-doctor crosses south-central Africa from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean with Makololo companions.
explorer.amundsen.name: Roald Amundsen
explorer.amundsen.title: The Race to the South Pole
explorer.amundsen.summary: A Norwegian polar explorer secretly turns south and races to be first at the South Pole.
threat.polo.name: The Great Sandstorm
threat.polo.desc: Moves faster over deserts and stalls in the mountains.
threat.magellan.name: The Portuguese Fleet
threat.magellan.desc: Moves faster in Portuguese waters and stops in the Pacific, where every node is a hazard instead (scurvy and thirst).
threat.livingstone.name: The Fever
threat.livingstone.desc: Moves faster along rivers, lakes and swamps; stalls in the highlands and the dry Kalahari.
threat.amundsen.name: The Polar Winter
threat.amundsen.desc: Stays still for two rounds, then surges 3 steps every third round.
ability.polo.name: Golden Paiza
ability.polo.desc: Once per act, after a wrong answer: cancel the penalty. The threat doesn't move this round and you still advance 1 step. (Kublai Khan gave the elder Polos a golden tablet of safe passage on their first journey.)
ability.magellan.name: Trade Winds
ability.magellan.desc: Once per act, declared before answering: a correct answer moves you double, a wrong one adds +1 to the threat.
ability.livingstone.name: Physician
ability.livingstone.desc: The first time each act you would lose a life, you don't (you still return to your checkpoint). Medicine Chests restore 2 lives.
ability.amundsen.name: Depot Laying
ability.amundsen.desc: After a correct answer you may store 1 step in your depot (up to 3) and spend depot steps when you plan a later turn.
node.polo.venice.name: Venice
node.polo.venice.note: Marco, aged 17, his father Niccolò and his uncle Maffeo set out for the court of Kublai Khan.
node.polo.eastern-med.name: Eastern Mediterranean
node.polo.eastern-med.note: The Polos sail from Venice to the crusader port of Acre.
node.polo.acre.name: Acre
node.polo.acre.note: Teobaldo Visconti, the papal legate in Acre, is elected Pope Gregory X and gives the Polos letters for Kublai.
node.polo.ayas.name: Ayas (Laiazzo)
node.polo.ayas.note: Port of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia. The two friars sent with the Polos lose heart and turn back.
node.polo.sivas.name: Sivas
node.polo.sivas.note: A city of "Turcomania" (Anatolia), whose carpets Polo calls the finest in the world.
node.polo.erzurum.name: Erzurum
node.polo.erzurum.note: In "Greater Armenia", a land of summer pastures and bitter winters.
node.polo.ararat.name: Near Mount Ararat
node.polo.ararat.note: Polo describes the great mountain "on which Noah's Ark is said to rest".
node.polo.tabriz.name: Tabriz
node.polo.tabriz.note: A great trading city of the Mongol Ilkhanate, where merchants from India, Baghdad and Europe meet.
node.polo.saveh.name: Saveh
node.polo.saveh.note: Polo reports a local tradition that the Three Magi set out from here, and are buried here.
node.polo.yazd.name: Yazd
node.polo.yazd.note: A desert city whose silk cloth, Polo says, merchants carry far and wide.
node.polo.kerman.name: Kerman
node.polo.kerman.note: Known to Polo for its turquoises and fine needlework.
node.polo.hormuz.name: Hormuz
node.polo.hormuz.note: The Polos come down to this port to sail for China, judge the ships unsafe, and turn back inland.
node.polo.kuhbanan.name: Kuhbanan (Cobinan)
node.polo.kuhbanan.note: After a hard desert crossing from Kerman, Polo describes the town's steel mirrors.
node.polo.balkh.name: Balkh
node.polo.balkh.note: "A noble city and a great", Polo writes, though it was wrecked by the Mongols in 1220.
node.polo.badakhshan.name: Badakhshan
node.polo.badakhshan.note: Polo writes that he spent about a year here recovering from illness. The region is famous for lapis lazuli and "balas rubies".
node.polo.wakhan.name: Wakhan
node.polo.wakhan.note: A high valley leading up into the Pamirs.
node.polo.pamir.name: The Pamir
node.polo.pamir.note: A plateau so high and cold, Polo says, that no birds fly and fire gives little heat.
node.polo.kashgar.name: Kashgar
node.polo.kashgar.note: A Silk Road oasis where the roads around the Taklamakan Desert divide.
node.polo.yarkand.name: Yarkand
node.polo.yarkand.note: An oasis on the southern Silk Road.
node.polo.khotan.name: Khotan
node.polo.khotan.note: Famous for jade, gathered from its rivers and carried to China.
node.polo.charchan.name: Charchan (Qiemo)
node.polo.charchan.note: Polo notes the jasper and chalcedony found in its rivers.
node.polo.lop.name: Lop
node.polo.lop.note: Travellers rest here before a month-long desert crossing. Polo tells of spirit voices that lure travellers away.
node.polo.aksu.name: Aksu
node.polo.aksu.note: An oasis on the northern Silk Road (not the Polos' route).
node.polo.kucha.name: Kucha
node.polo.kucha.note: A Buddhist oasis kingdom on the northern Silk Road (not the Polos' route).
node.polo.korla.name: Korla
node.polo.korla.note: An oasis on the northern Silk Road (not the Polos' route).
node.polo.turpan.name: Turpan
node.polo.turpan.note: An oasis famous for grapes and underground karez channels (not the Polos' route).
node.polo.hami.name: Hami (Kumul)
node.polo.hami.note: The last oasis of the northern road before Gansu (not the Polos' route).
node.polo.shazhou.name: Shazhou (Dunhuang)
node.polo.shazhou.note: Polo describes the town's many Buddhist temples.
node.polo.ganzhou.name: Ganzhou (Zhangye)
node.polo.ganzhou.note: Polo writes that the family stayed here for a year on business.
node.polo.shangdu.name: Shangdu (Xanadu)
node.polo.shangdu.note: The Polos reach Kublai Khan at his summer capital, about three and a half years after leaving Venice.
node.magellan.sanlucar.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda
node.magellan.sanlucar.note: 20 September 1519: five ships and about 270 men leave Spain to find a western route to the Spice Islands.
node.magellan.tenerife.name: Tenerife
node.magellan.tenerife.note: The fleet takes on water and supplies in the Canary Islands.
node.magellan.cape-verde-pass.name: Off Cape Verde
node.magellan.cape-verde-pass.note: Magellan steers south along the African coast instead of crossing directly.
node.magellan.sierra-leone.name: Off Sierra Leone
node.magellan.sierra-leone.note: Storms and calms off Guinea. The Spanish captain Juan de Cartagena protests at the course and is relieved of command.
node.magellan.atlantic-crossing.name: Crossing the Atlantic
node.magellan.atlantic-crossing.note: The fleet finally turns west towards Brazil.
node.magellan.open-atlantic.name: Open Atlantic
node.magellan.open-atlantic.note: The usual course south-west, where Portuguese ships might be waiting (not Magellan's route).
node.magellan.equator.name: Crossing the Equator
node.magellan.equator.note: The usual crossing point on the direct course (not Magellan's route).
node.magellan.brazil-coast.name: Coast of Brazil
node.magellan.brazil-coast.note: November 1519: first sight of South America, near Cape Santo Agostinho.
node.magellan.rio.name: Bay of Rio de Janeiro
node.magellan.rio.note: December 1519: the fleet rests in the bay it names Santa Lucía.
node.magellan.plata.name: Río de la Plata
node.magellan.plata.note: January 1520: Magellan explores the wide estuary, hoping it is the passage west.
node.magellan.san-julian.name: Puerto San Julián
node.magellan.san-julian.note: The fleet winters here. In April 1520 three captains mutiny and Magellan crushes the revolt.
node.magellan.santa-cruz.name: Santa Cruz
node.magellan.santa-cruz.note: May 1520: the Santiago is wrecked while scouting the coast. Its crew survives.
node.magellan.virgins.name: Cape of the Virgins
node.magellan.virgins.note: 21 October 1520: the fleet finds the entrance to the strait.
node.magellan.strait.name: Strait of Magellan
node.magellan.strait.note: Five weeks threading the channels. The San Antonio deserts and sails back to Spain.
node.magellan.pacific-east.name: Pacific Ocean
node.magellan.pacific-east.note: December 1520: the fleet heads north-west into an ocean far larger than anyone expected.
node.magellan.pacific-west.name: Crossing the Pacific
node.magellan.pacific-west.note: Months without fresh food or water. Many die of scurvy.
node.magellan.guam.name: Guam
node.magellan.guam.note: 6 March 1521: first landfall after crossing the Pacific.
node.magellan.limasawa.name: Limasawa
node.magellan.limasawa.note: March 1521: first contact in the Philippines. The first Mass is traditionally placed here, on Easter Sunday.
node.magellan.cebu.name: Cebu
node.magellan.cebu.note: April 1521: the ruler Humabon is baptised. On 27 April Magellan is killed fighting on nearby Mactan.
node.magellan.palawan.name: Palawan
node.magellan.palawan.note: The survivors, now on two ships, search for food and the way to the Spice Islands.
node.magellan.brunei.name: Brunei
node.magellan.brunei.note: July 1521: the expedition visits the wealthy sultanate on Borneo.
node.magellan.tidore.name: Tidore
node.magellan.tidore.note: November 1521: the Spice Islands at last. The Victoria, under Juan Sebastián Elcano, will sail home westward.
node.magellan.timor.name: Timor
node.magellan.timor.note: The last landfall before crossing the Indian Ocean.
node.magellan.indian-ocean.name: Southern Indian Ocean
node.magellan.indian-ocean.note: To avoid the Portuguese, the Victoria sails far south, away from all ports. Food runs out.
node.magellan.good-hope.name: Cape of Good Hope
node.magellan.good-hope.note: May 1522: after weeks of storms, the Victoria rounds the Cape.
node.magellan.cape-verde.name: Santiago, Cape Verde
node.magellan.cape-verde.note: July 1522: a stop for food at a Portuguese colony. Thirteen men are held, and the "lost day" is discovered.
node.magellan.sanlucar-return.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda
node.magellan.sanlucar-return.note: 6 September 1522: the Victoria returns with 18 men, the first ship to sail around the world.
node.livingstone.cape-town.name: Cape Town
node.livingstone.cape-town.note: June 1852: Livingstone sends his family to Britain and sets out north.
node.livingstone.kuruman.name: Kuruman
node.livingstone.kuruman.note: The mission of Robert Moffat, Livingstone's father-in-law, on the edge of the Kalahari.
node.livingstone.kalahari-south.name: The Kalahari
node.livingstone.kalahari-south.note: The wagon road north crosses dry Kalahari country, where water is scarce.
node.livingstone.kalahari-north.name: Northern Kalahari
node.livingstone.kalahari-north.note: Slow progress by ox-wagon towards the Chobe River.
node.livingstone.chobe.name: Chobe River
node.livingstone.chobe.note: The wagons reach the river country of the Makololo.
node.livingstone.linyanti.name: Linyanti
node.livingstone.linyanti.note: May 1853: the Makololo capital. Chief Sekeletu provides men for a journey to the west coast.
node.livingstone.sesheke.name: Sesheke
node.livingstone.sesheke.note: November 1853: Livingstone and 27 Makololo set off up the Zambezi by canoe.
node.livingstone.barotse.name: Barotse Valley
node.livingstone.barotse.note: The Zambezi floodplain of the Lozi people.
node.livingstone.dilolo.name: Lake Dilolo
node.livingstone.dilolo.note: February 1854: Livingstone realises he is standing on the watershed between the Zambezi and Congo basins.
node.livingstone.kasai.name: Kasai River
node.livingstone.kasai.note: Great river crossings, and fever again and again.
node.livingstone.kwango.name: Kwango River
node.livingstone.kwango.note: April 1854: the exhausted party crosses the Kwango into Portuguese territory.
node.livingstone.cassange.name: Cassange (Kasanje)
node.livingstone.cassange.note: A Portuguese trading post, the first since the interior.
node.livingstone.luanda.name: Luanda
node.livingstone.luanda.note: 31 May 1854: Livingstone reaches the Atlantic, gravely ill.
node.livingstone.return-angola.name: The road back through Angola
node.livingstone.return-angola.note: 1854–1855: Livingstone keeps his promise and leads the Makololo home.
node.livingstone.return-barotse.name: Back up the Zambezi
node.livingstone.return-barotse.note: 1855: the party returns through the Barotse Valley.
node.livingstone.linyanti-return.name: Linyanti
node.livingstone.linyanti-return.note: September 1855: back at the Makololo capital.
node.livingstone.victoria-falls.name: Victoria Falls
node.livingstone.victoria-falls.note: 16 November 1855: Livingstone sees Mosi-oa-Tunya and names it after Queen Victoria.
node.livingstone.batoka.name: Batoka Plateau
node.livingstone.batoka.note: Livingstone leaves the river and crosses the healthier highlands.
node.livingstone.kafue.name: Kafue River
node.livingstone.kafue.note: The party crosses the Kafue near where it joins the Zambezi.
node.livingstone.zumbo.name: Zumbo
node.livingstone.zumbo.note: January 1856: the ruins of an old Portuguese trading station.
node.livingstone.overland.name: North of the river
node.livingstone.overland.note: Livingstone continues overland, away from the river, and misses the Kebrabasa rapids.
node.livingstone.batoka-gorge.name: Batoka Gorge
node.livingstone.batoka-gorge.note: The Zambezi rushes through deep gorges below the falls (not Livingstone's route on this journey).
node.livingstone.kariba-gorge.name: Kariba Gorge
node.livingstone.kariba-gorge.note: A narrow gorge where the river cuts through the hills (not Livingstone's route on this journey).
node.livingstone.kebrabasa.name: Kebrabasa Rapids
node.livingstone.kebrabasa.note: Rapids that block boats on the Zambezi. Livingstone only discovered them on his next expedition, in 1858.
node.livingstone.tete.name: Tete
node.livingstone.tete.note: March 1856: a Portuguese town on the Zambezi. Most of the Makololo stay here to await his return.
node.livingstone.lower-zambezi.name: Lower Zambezi
node.livingstone.lower-zambezi.note: Down the river towards the coast.
node.livingstone.quelimane.name: Quelimane
node.livingstone.quelimane.note: 20 May 1856: the Indian Ocean. Livingstone has crossed Africa from coast to coast.
node.amundsen.kristiania.name: Kristiania (Oslo)
node.amundsen.kristiania.note: June 1910: Fram leaves, officially bound for the Arctic.
node.amundsen.kristiansand.name: Kristiansand
node.amundsen.kristiansand.note: 9 August 1910: Fram's final departure from Norway.
node.amundsen.north-sea.name: North Sea
node.amundsen.north-sea.note: Fram, built to drift in pack ice, rolls heavily in the open sea.
node.amundsen.biscay.name: Bay of Biscay
node.amundsen.biscay.note: Rough water on the way south.
node.amundsen.madeira.name: Funchal, Madeira
node.amundsen.madeira.note: September 1910: Amundsen tells the crew they are going to the South Pole.
node.amundsen.off-africa.name: Off West Africa
node.amundsen.equator.name: Crossing the Equator
node.amundsen.south-atlantic.name: South Atlantic
node.amundsen.roaring-forties.name: The Roaring Forties
node.amundsen.roaring-forties.note: Fram runs east before the great westerly winds.
node.amundsen.south-of-cape.name: South of the Cape of Good Hope
node.amundsen.south-of-cape.note: Fram passes far south of Africa.
node.amundsen.south-indian.name: Southern Indian Ocean
node.amundsen.south-indian.note: Weeks of gales in the high southern latitudes.
node.amundsen.south-of-australia.name: South of Australia
node.amundsen.south-of-australia.note: Fram sails on east, far south of Australia and New Zealand.
node.amundsen.ross-pack.name: Ross Sea pack ice
node.amundsen.ross-pack.note: January 1911: Fram pushes through the pack ice.
node.amundsen.framheim.name: Framheim, Bay of Whales
node.amundsen.framheim.note: 14 January 1911: the base is built on the Ross Ice Shelf.
node.amundsen.depot-80.name: Depot at 80° S
node.amundsen.depot-80.note: Laid in February 1911. The polar party set out on 20 October 1911.
node.amundsen.depot-81.name: Depot at 81° S
node.amundsen.depot-81.note: One of the supply depots laid before the winter.
node.amundsen.depot-82.name: Depot at 82° S
node.amundsen.depot-82.note: The southernmost depot laid before the winter.
node.amundsen.depot-83.name: Depot at 83° S
node.amundsen.depot-83.note: On the way south, Amundsen lays a small depot at every degree of latitude.
node.amundsen.depot-84.name: Depot at 84° S
node.amundsen.queen-maud.name: Queen Maud Mountains
node.amundsen.queen-maud.note: November 1911: the party reaches the mountains at about 85° S.
node.amundsen.axel-heiberg.name: Axel Heiberg Glacier
node.amundsen.axel-heiberg.note: An unknown glacier. The dogs haul the sledges up to the plateau in a few days.
node.amundsen.devils-ballroom.name: The Devil's Ballroom
node.amundsen.devils-ballroom.note: A crevassed surface at the edge of the plateau, crossed in fog.
node.amundsen.ross-shelf-west.name: Western Ross Ice Shelf
node.amundsen.ross-shelf-west.note: Shackleton's 1908 route, which Scott followed in 1911–12 (not Amundsen's route).
node.amundsen.gateway.name: The Gateway
node.amundsen.gateway.note: Shackleton's way from the ice shelf onto the Beardmore Glacier (not Amundsen's route).
node.amundsen.beardmore-lower.name: Lower Beardmore Glacier
node.amundsen.beardmore-lower.note: One of the largest valley glaciers in the world (not Amundsen's route).
node.amundsen.cloudmaker.name: Mount Cloudmaker
node.amundsen.cloudmaker.note: A landmark peak beside the Beardmore Glacier (not Amundsen's route).
node.amundsen.beardmore-upper.name: Upper Beardmore Glacier
node.amundsen.beardmore-upper.note: The long climb towards the plateau (not Amundsen's route).
node.amundsen.plateau-west.name: Polar Plateau (west)
node.amundsen.plateau-west.note: Where Shackleton turned back in 1909, 180 km from the Pole (not Amundsen's route).
node.amundsen.polar-plateau.name: Polar Plateau
node.amundsen.polar-plateau.note: December 1911: the last stretch, at nearly 3,000 m.
node.amundsen.south-pole.name: South Pole (Polheim)
node.amundsen.south-pole.note: 14 December 1911: Amundsen, Bjaaland, Hanssen, Hassel and Wisting reach the Pole.
fork.polo.tarim.question: Which road around the Taklamakan Desert?
fork.polo.tarim.truth: The Polos took the southern road through Yarkand, Khotan and Lop. The northern road through Kucha and Turpan was the other main Silk Road branch of the time.
fork.polo.tarim.south.name: The southern road (Khotan, Lop)
fork.polo.tarim.south.desc: Shorter, through desert oases. The desert of Lop is a hazard.
fork.polo.tarim.north.name: The northern road (Kucha, Turpan)
fork.polo.tarim.north.desc: Longer, from oasis to oasis along the Tian Shan.
fork.magellan.atlantic.question: How to cross the Atlantic?
fork.magellan.atlantic.truth: Magellan followed the African coast south before crossing. Juan de Cartagena protested against the unusual course and was relieved of his command.
fork.magellan.atlantic.coast.name: South along the African coast
fork.magellan.atlantic.coast.desc: Longer, but away from the usual course where Portuguese ships might wait.
fork.magellan.atlantic.direct.name: The direct crossing
fork.magellan.atlantic.direct.desc: The usual course: shorter, but through Portuguese waters.
fork.livingstone.batoka.question: Follow the Zambezi or cross the plateau?
fork.livingstone.batoka.truth: Livingstone left the river and crossed the plateau. So he never saw the Kebrabasa rapids, which later wrecked his plan to use the Zambezi as a navigable highway into Africa.
fork.livingstone.batoka.plateau.name: Over the Batoka plateau
fork.livingstone.batoka.river.name: Down the Zambezi gorges
fork.livingstone.batoka.river.desc: Shorter, along the river: fever country and dangerous rapids.
fork.amundsen.pole.question: Which way up to the Polar Plateau?
fork.amundsen.pole.truth: Amundsen struck straight south from the Bay of Whales and found the Axel Heiberg Glacier. Scott, starting from Ross Island, took Shackleton's Beardmore route and reached the Pole 34 days after Amundsen.
fork.amundsen.pole.axel-heiberg.name: Amundsen's gamble: an unknown glacier
fork.amundsen.pole.axel-heiberg.desc: Shorter but unexplored: crevasses and steep ice.
fork.amundsen.pole.beardmore.name: The known road: the Beardmore Glacier
fork.amundsen.pole.beardmore.desc: Longer, along the route Shackleton found in 1908.
notes.polo.1: The route follows Marco Polo's own account, The Travels. Some stages are reconstructed by historians and are still debated.
notes.polo.2: Places on the route are ones Polo describes; steps do not reflect distance or time.
notes.polo.3: Dates marked "c." are approximate. The departure (1271) and arrival (1275) are documented.
notes.polo.4: The Great Sandstorm dramatises the real dangers of the desert crossings.
notes.magellan.1: Ocean nodes such as "Pacific Ocean" mark the fleet's track, not ports.
notes.magellan.2: After Magellan's death the expedition was led by several men in turn; your token continues as the expedition, later under Elcano.
notes.magellan.3: King Manuel I of Portugal really ordered the fleet to be intercepted. The pursuing Portuguese Fleet dramatises that danger.
notes.magellan.4: The "direct crossing" branch is the usual course that Magellan chose not to take.
notes.livingstone.1: The return journey from Luanda to Linyanti (1854–1855) is shortened to three nodes.
notes.livingstone.2: The Kalahari crossing of 1852–53 is shown by two nodes.
notes.livingstone.3: The Fever stands for the malaria attacks Livingstone suffered throughout the journey.
notes.livingstone.4: The "Zambezi gorges" branch shows the river route he did not take.
notes.amundsen.1: Fram sailed from Madeira to the Bay of Whales without landing; ocean nodes mark positions on her track.
notes.amundsen.2: The depots at 80–82° S were laid in February–March 1911; the dates shown are when the polar party passed them.
notes.amundsen.3: The Polar Winter stands for the race against the seasons.
notes.amundsen.4: The Beardmore branch is the route Scott took, not Amundsen's.
